Feature collapse asymmetry in self-supervised contrastive learning asks: when hard negative mining curricula prevent dimensional collapse in some feature subspaces while inadvertently accelerating it in others, what governs that asymmetry and can it be controlled? The key concepts are (1) dimensional collapse — the tendency of contrastive encoders to use only a low-dimensional subspace of the embedding space; (2) hard negative mining — preferentially sampling negatives close to the anchor in embedding space to sharpen gradients; and (3) curriculum — scheduling the difficulty of those negatives over training. The asymmetry emerges because hard negatives that are informative for one semantic axis are trivial for another: mining near the anchor in a high-curvature region of the manifold generates strong gradient signal along the dominant eigendirections of the feature covariance while starving the low-variance directions of useful signal, causing selective collapse. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is gradient anisotropy compounding over training — each round of hard negative selection is conditioned on the current encoder, so the mining distribution and the collapse geometry co-evolve in a feedback loop; by the time collapse is detectable in a low-eigenvalue tail, the curriculum has already locked the encoder into a basin that resists correction through naive regularization like uniformity losses.

The cleanest external signal is a small frozen probe dataset with known class structure that is orthogonal to the pretraining distribution — if a collapsed dimension carries zero linear separability on this probe set throughout training, it is likely genuinely uninformative; if separability is nonzero but flat, it is undertrained. Tian et al. (2021, "Understanding Self-Supervised Learning Dynamics") showed that probing intermediate representations every few hundred steps reveals that different semantic axes become linearly decodable at different training times, with some dimensions not activating until after 60% of training — so early flatness is not diagnostic of permanent uninformativeness. An architectural constraint that partially breaks the ambiguity is feature decorrelation with a delayed or annealed strength, as in the off-diagonal penalty in Barlow Twins (Zbontar et al. 2021): by forcing decorrelation weakly early and strongly late, you give undertrained dimensions time to accumulate signal before the penalty treats their low variance as redundancy to eliminate. However, there is a regime where the ambiguity is unresolvable in principle: when the pretraining data manifold has intrinsic dimensionality lower than the embedding space, some dimensions must be uninformative by the data geometry itself, and no amount of training or probing can distinguish these from collapsed-but-recoverable dimensions without either labeled data or a generative model of the true manifold. This is not merely a practical limitation — it is a formal identifiability problem analogous to the indeterminacy of ICA when source distributions are Gaussian, and it implies that for sufficiently low-dimensional data (e.g., synthetic datasets like CIFAR-10, estimated intrinsic dimension ~14–20 per Ansuini et al. 2019, embedded in 2048-dimensional spaces) a large fraction of collapsed dimensions are ambiguous by construction and the curriculum cannot be corrected without external supervision.

There is an implied optimal embedding dimension, but it sits above the data manifold's intrinsic dimensionality rather than at it — the reason is that contrastive objectives need slack dimensions to handle augmentation variance, class boundary curvature, and the mismatch between pretraining and downstream task geometry; empirically, Chen et al. (2020) found SimCLR performance peaks around 128–256 dimensions on ImageNet even though estimated intrinsic dimensionality of ImageNet is roughly 40–50 (Pope et al. 2021), suggesting a practical multiplier of 3–5× over intrinsic dimension. Under-parameterizing the projection head relative to intrinsic dimension is acutely damaging: the encoder is forced to compress semantically distinct directions into shared dimensions, producing entangled representations that transfer poorly to tasks requiring fine-grained discrimination — Tian et al. Over-parameterizing produces a subtler failure: the projection head absorbs task-relevant variance that should propagate into the backbone, a phenomenon Bordes et al. (2023) called "dimensional absorption," where the head learns to span the informative subspace and the backbone representations become shallower and less transferable — this is why the standard practice of discarding the projection head at transfer time (introduced in SimCLR) is not merely conventional but mechanistically necessary. The critical non-obvious interaction with hard negative curricula is that over-parameterized heads shift the collapse asymmetry: more head dimensions means the mining geometry is computed in a higher-dimensional space where hard negatives are sparser (curse of dimensionality), reducing mining pressure and partially alleviating asymmetric collapse in the backbone — but at the cost of making the head's geometry increasingly decoupled from the backbone's, so the diagnostic signals discussed earlier (eigenspectrum monitoring, effective rank) become misleading if computed at the head rather than the backbone.

The most direct approach is to compute the hard negative similarity kernel at an intermediate backbone layer — say, after the third residual block in a ResNet-50 — and use that score for mining while optimizing the full network end-to-end; this is structurally similar to what Kalantidis et al. The failure mode specific to backbone-locus mining is representation rigidity: because the mining distribution now directly depends on backbone geometry, gradient updates that would reorganize the backbone's eigendirections are resisted — the backbone becomes self-referentially locked, analogous to a fixed-point attractor, and learning rate warmup schedules must be significantly extended (roughly 2–3× standard warmup) to avoid premature convergence to a suboptimal fixed point. The deeper unresolved tension is that any procedure making the backbone the locus of geometric correction reintroduces the head-discarding problem in a new form: the backbone's geometry at transfer time reflects the mining pressure it was subjected to, which was shaped by the pretraining task's negative structure, not the downstream task's discriminative requirements.

Random negative injection does function as a geometric perturbation, but the mechanism is more specific than simply "adding noise" — random negatives sample uniformly from the data manifold and therefore have expected cosine similarity close to zero in a well-initialized embedding space, meaning their gradients push isotropically on the uniformity term rather than reinforcing dominant eigendirections, which is precisely the corrective pressure needed to counteract fixed-point lock-in. The mixing ratio problem has a principled solution grounded in gradient variance equalization: you want the gradient magnitude contributed by random negatives to match the gradient magnitude in the lowest-variance eigendirections produced by hard negatives, which you can estimate from the eigenspectrum of the hard negative batch covariance computed at the backbone — in practice this yields random negative fractions in the 15–30% range for ResNet-50 on ImageNet, consistent with the empirical finding in Robinson et al. (2021) that a debiased correction term of roughly 20% random negatives recovered ~2 points of linear probe accuracy lost to false-negative contamination. The critical implementation detail is that the mixing ratio must be adaptive and eigenspectrum-conditioned rather than fixed: early in training when hard negatives are not yet geometrically concentrated, a high random fraction (30–40%) wastes gradient budget on easy negatives; as the backbone geometry sharpens and hard negative concentration increases (detectable via the effective rank drop discussed earlier), the random fraction should decrease to maintain gradient efficiency while the perturbative role diminishes because the attractor basin hasn't yet formed. The failure mode of getting this schedule wrong in the downward direction — reducing random negatives too fast — is precisely gradient starvation in low-variance dimensions, and it is insidious because the eigenspectrum metric that tells you to reduce random negatives is the same metric that warns of impending collapse, creating a control ambiguity. A practical resolution is to treat the random fraction as a PID-controlled parameter with the effective rank ratio (hard negative effective rank / random negative effective rank) as the process variable and a target ratio near 0.85 as the setpoint — this has not been published as a complete system but the components exist in separate works (eigenspectrum monitoring in Garrido et al. 2023, adaptive curriculum pacing in Wu et al. 2020) and the control-theoretic framing converts an open-loop scheduling guess into a closed-loop correction.

More practically, early-layer activation statistics from the first one or two convolutional layers — which are minimally affected by the contrastive objective because gradients attenuate through depth — can serve as a proxy for input geometry; the effective rank of layer-1 feature maps on a held-out batch is nearly backbone-independent and tracks input manifold dimensionality to within ~10% in ResNet architectures (Raghu et al. 2017 showed activation dimensionality in early layers is stable across very different training regimes).
